pairs.source_text: Athenis mutabo ita ut hoc est proscaenium tantisper dum transigimus hanc comoediam.
pairs.question: In qua urbe fabula Plauti Truculentus, mutato in prologo proscaenio, agitur?
pairs.question_en: In what city is Plautus' play Truculentus set, the prologue turning the stage-front into it?
pairs.derivation: The prologue transforms the stage into Athens for the duration of the play. Anchored to the named play; one-word place answer verbatim (Athenis mutabo).

pairs.source_text: nam mihi haec meretrix quae hic habet, Phronesium, suom nomen omne ex pectore exmovit meo, phronesim, nam phronesis est sapientia.
pairs.question: Quid significat nomen meretricis Phronesii apud Plautum in Truculento, ut Diniarchus ludens explicat?
pairs.question_en: What does the name of the courtesan Phronesium mean in Plautus' Truculentus, as Diniarchus playfully explains?
pairs.derivation: A name-etymology fact: Phronesium's name is the Greek phronesis, 'wisdom/prudence'; Diniarchus puns that she drove all his phronesis out of his heart. Anchored to Phronesium + Truculentus; one-word answer verbatim (phronesis est sapientia).

pairs.source_text: Tres unam pereunt adulescentes mulierem. Rure unus, alter urbe, peregre tertius;
pairs.question: Quot amatores simul Phronesium meretrix in Truculento Plauti emungit atque perdit?
pairs.question_en: How many lovers does the courtesan Phronesium fleece and ruin at once in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: The play's premise: three young men are ruined for one woman, one from the country, one from the city, one from abroad. Anchored to Phronesium + Truculentus; number answer verbatim (Tres unam pereunt adulescentes mulierem).

pairs.source_text: ea se peperisse puerum simulat militi, quo citius rem ab eo averrat cum pulvisculo.
pairs.question: Quid Phronesium meretrix militi se fecisse simulat, ut eius rem citius auferat, apud Plautum in Truculento?
pairs.question_en: What does the courtesan Phronesium pretend to have done with respect to the soldier, in order to sweep away his money the faster, in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.answer_en: To have borne him a son.
pairs.derivation: The suppositious-child scheme, the play's central trick: Phronesium pretends to have borne the soldier a boy to extract greater gifts. Anchored to Phronesium + Truculentus; short answer verbatim (se peperisse puerum simulat militi).

pairs.source_text: quem antehac odiosum sibi esse memorabat mala, Babyloniensem militem. is nunc dicitur venturus peregre;
pairs.question: Quali cognomine Diniarchus rivalem suum, militem peregre venientem amatorem Phronesii, in Truculento Plauti designat?
pairs.question_en: By what epithet does Diniarchus designate his rival, the soldier-lover of Phronesium coming from abroad, in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: The braggart-soldier lover serving abroad: Diniarchus' rival is 'the Babylonian soldier,' returning from overseas with plunder-gifts. Anchored to Phronesium + Truculentus; short answer verbatim (Babyloniensem militem).

pairs.source_text: meretricem sentis similem esse condecet, quemquem hominem attigerit, profecto ei aut malum aut damnum dare.
pairs.question: Cui rei spinosae Astaphium ancilla meretricem similem esse oportere dicit, quae cuique quem attingit malum aut damnum dat, in Truculento Plauti?
pairs.question_en: To what thorny thing does the maid Astaphium say a courtesan ought to be similar, one who gives harm or loss to whomever she touches, in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: Astaphium's maxim on the trade: a courtesan should be like a bramble, harming whatever she touches. Anchored to Astaphium + Truculentus; one-word answer verbatim (meretricem sentis similem esse).

pairs.source_text: Amator similest oppidi hostilis. DIN. Quo argumento est? AST. Quam primum expugnari potis est, tam id optimum est amicae.
pairs.question: Cui loco Astaphium amatorem similem esse dicit, quem quam primum 'expugnari' amicae optimum est, in Truculento Plauti?
pairs.question_en: To what place does Astaphium liken a lover, one whom it is best for the courtesan to 'storm' as soon as possible, in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: Astaphium's simile: a lover is like an enemy town, best sacked quickly. Anchored to Astaphium + Truculentus; short answer verbatim (Amator similest oppidi hostilis).

pairs.source_text: nimis quidem hic truculentust.
pairs.question: Quo cognomine appellatur servus ille agrestis et violentus a quo comoedia Plauti nomen accepit?
pairs.question_en: By what epithet is that boorish, violent slave called, the one from whom Plautus' comedy takes its name?
pairs.derivation: The title-character: a churlish country slave whom Astaphium dubs 'truculentus,' and who gives the play its name. Anchored to the named play; one-word answer verbatim (nimis quidem hic truculentust).

pairs.source_text: Erilis noster filius apud vos Strabax ut pereat, ut eum inliciatis in malam fraudem et probrum.
pairs.question: Cuius domini sui filium, adulescentem rusticum, servus truculentus apud meretrices perire dolet in Truculento Plauti?
pairs.question_en: Which son of his master, a rustic young man, does the churlish slave grieve to see ruined among the courtesans in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: The churlish slave's grievance identifies the country lover: Strabax, the young master whose money is being drained at Phronesium's. Anchored to the slave + Truculentus; one-name answer verbatim (erilis noster filius ... Strabax).

pairs.source_text: pluris est oculatus testis unus quam auriti decem; qui audiunt audita dicunt, qui vident plane sciunt.
pairs.question: Quot testibus 'auritis' unum testem 'oculatum' Stratophanes miles apud Plautum in Truculento pluris esse dicit?
pairs.question_en: Than how many 'ear-witnesses' does the soldier Stratophanes say one 'eyewitness' is worth more, in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: The proverb of the eyewitness: one who sees is worth more than ten who merely hear. Anchored to the named play; number answer verbatim (oculatus testis unus quam auriti decem).

pairs.source_text: Miles, mea Phronesium, tibi adest Stratophanes.
pairs.question: Quod est nomen militis, amatoris Phronesii, qui peregre cum donis exoticis Athenas revenit in Truculento Plauti?
pairs.question_en: What is the name of the soldier, Phronesium's lover, who returns to Athens from abroad with exotic gifts in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: The braggart-soldier lover named: Stratophanes, back from the wars to claim the son Phronesium pretends she bore him. Anchored to Phronesium + Truculentus; one-name answer verbatim (tibi adest Stratophanes).

pairs.source_text: adduxi ancillas tibi eccas ex Suria duas, is te dono. adduce hoc tu istas. sed istae reginae domi suae fuerunt ambae, earum patriam ego excidi manu.
pairs.question: Ex qua terra duas ancillas, olim reginas, Stratophanes miles Phronesio dono adducit in Truculento Plauti?
pairs.question_en: From what land does the soldier Stratophanes bring two slave-maids, once queens, as a gift to Phronesium in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: The braggart soldier's plunder-gifts from abroad: two Syrian slave-women, said to have been queens whose homeland he sacked. Anchored to Stratophanes + Truculentus; place answer verbatim (ancillas ... ex Suria duas).

pairs.source_text: ex Arabia tibi attuli tus, Ponto amomum. tene tibi, voluptas mea.
pairs.question: Vnde tus, quod Stratophanes miles Phronesio dono attulit, oriundum esse in Truculento Plauti dicitur?
pairs.question_en: From where does the frankincense that the soldier Stratophanes brings Phronesium as a gift come, in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: Among the soldier's exotic gifts, frankincense from Arabia (the ambient association of Arabia with incense) and amomum from Pontus. Anchored to Stratophanes + Truculentus; place answer verbatim (ex Arabia ... tus).

pairs.source_text: date mi huc stactam atque ignem in aram, ut venerem Lucinam meam.
pairs.question: Quam deam Phronesium, puerperium mentita, apud Plautum in Truculento veneratur?
pairs.question_en: What goddess does Phronesium worship, feigning childbirth, in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: Lucina, the Roman goddess of childbirth, invoked by Phronesium to make her fake lying-in convincing. Anchored to Phronesium + Truculentus; one-name answer verbatim (venerem Lucinam meam).

pairs.source_text: Mars peregre adveniens salutat Nerienem uxorem suam.
pairs.question: Cuius dei uxor Nerienes (Nerio) habebatur, quam Stratophanes miles, se Martem fingens, apud Plautum in Truculento salutat?
pairs.question_en: Of what god was Nerio (Nerienes) held to be the wife, whom the soldier Stratophanes, playing Mars, greets in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: Roman divine lore: Nerio (Nerienes) was the consort of Mars; the swaggering soldier greets Phronesium as 'Mars greeting his wife Nerio.' Anchored to the named play; one-name answer verbatim (Mars ... salutat Nerienem uxorem suam).

pairs.source_text: meretricem ego item esse reor, mare ut est: quod des devorat nec datis umquam abundat.
pairs.question: Cui rei Cyamus servus meretricem similem esse dicit, quae quod datur devorat neque umquam datis abundat, in Truculento Plauti?
pairs.question_en: To what does the slave Cyamus liken a courtesan, one who swallows whatever is given and is never full from the giving, in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: Cyamus' simile on the trade: a courtesan is like the sea, devouring all gifts yet never full. Anchored to Cyamus + Truculentus; one-word answer verbatim (meretricem ... esse reor, mare ut est).

pairs.source_text: qui ovis Tarentinas erat mercatus de patre.
pairs.question: Cuius generis oves ille debitor a patre Strabacis emerat, quarum pretium Strabax ad Phronesium defert in Truculento Plauti?
pairs.question_en: What kind of sheep had that debtor bought from Strabax's father, whose price Strabax carries off to Phronesium in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: Livestock- and wool-trade realia: the prized Tarentine sheep, famed for fine wool. Their sale-price is what the country lover Strabax squanders on the courtesan. Anchored to Strabax + Truculentus; answer verbatim (ovis Tarentinas ... mercatus de patre).

pairs.source_text: Nimio minus saevos iam sum, Astaphium, quam fui, iam non ego sum truculentus, noli metuere.
pairs.question: Quomodo servi truculenti mores mutantur, postquam saepe in urbem ventitat, in Truculento Plauti?
pairs.question_en: How do the churlish slave's manners change once he keeps coming to the city, in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: The play's thematic point: the boorish country slave is tamed by city ways, declaring 'iam non sum truculentus' and that he has all new manners. Anchored to the title-slave + Truculentus; short answer supported verbatim (minus saevos iam sum ... iam non sum truculentus).

pairs.source_text: rabonem habeto, ut mecum hanc noctem sies. AST. Perii, rabonem? quam esse dicam hanc beluam? quin tu arrabonem dicis?
pairs.question: Quo nomine appellatur pignus pecuniae quod Stratophanes miles dat, ut secum Astaphium noctem sit, in Truculento Plauti?
pairs.question_en: By what name is the money-pledge called that the soldier Stratophanes gives so that Astaphium will spend the night with him, in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: Commercial realia: the arrabo, an earnest-money deposit sealing a bargain; the soldier pays one to reserve a night (comically clipping it to 'rabo'). Anchored to Stratophanes + Truculentus; one-word answer verbatim (arrabonem dicis).

pairs.source_text: Quid puero factumst, mea quem peperit filia, meo nepote? capita rerum ede expedite.
pairs.question: Cuius revera filia puerum peperit, quem Phronesium pro suo supposuit, in Truculento Plauti?
pairs.question_en: Whose daughter really bore the boy that Phronesium passed off as her own, in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: The recognition: the suppositious baby is truly the child of the old man Callicles' daughter, his grandson (meo nepote). Anchored to Callicles + Truculentus; one-name answer verbatim (mea quem peperit filia, meo nepote).

pairs.source_text: Diniarchus, quoi illam prius desponderas.
pairs.question: Cui adulescenti Callicles filiam suam desponderat, qui idem patrem pueri suppositi se esse in Truculento Plauti confitetur?
pairs.question_en: To what young man had Callicles betrothed his daughter, the same man who confesses to being the father of the suppositious child in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: The recognition resolving the plot: Diniarchus, betrothed to Callicles' daughter, is exposed as the man who violated her and fathered the child Phronesium passed off. Anchored to Callicles + Truculentus; one-name answer verbatim (Diniarchus, quoi illam prius desponderas).

pairs.source_text: verum hoc ego te multabo bolo: sex talenta magna dotis demam pro ista inscitia.
pairs.question: Quot talenta magna dotis Callicles Diniarcho detrahit, quod filiam eius ante nuptias vitiaverat, in Truculento Plauti?
pairs.question_en: How many great talents of dowry does Callicles deduct from Diniarchus, because he had violated his daughter before marriage, in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: The resolution's dowry realia: Callicles gives his daughter to Diniarchus but docks six talents from her dowry as a fine for the wrong. Anchored to Callicles + Diniarchus + Truculentus; number answer verbatim (sex talenta magna dotis demam).

pairs.source_text: Callicles, vide in quaestione ne facias iniuriam: reus solutus causam dicit, testis vinctos attines.
pairs.question: Quo statu reus in quaestione causam dicere solet, ut ancilla apud Plautum in Truculento Calliclem monet?
pairs.question_en: In what state does the accused (reus) usually plead his case in an inquiry, as the maid reminds Callicles in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: Roman legal-procedure realia: the accused pleads unbound, unlike the bound (torturable) slave-witnesses; the maid protests being kept bound while a reus would be free. Anchored to Truculentus; one-word answer verbatim (reus solutus causam dicit).

pairs.source_text: verum est verbum quod memoratur: ubi amici ibidem sunt opes.
pairs.question: Quid ibidem esse, ubi amici sint, proverbium a Phronesio apud Plautum in Truculento memoratum affirmat?
pairs.question_en: What does the proverb recalled by Phronesium in Plautus' Truculentus affirm to be present where friends are?
pairs.derivation: The proverb 'ubi amici ibi opes' — where there are friends, there is wealth. Anchored to Truculentus; one-word answer verbatim (ubi amici ibidem sunt opes).

pairs.source_text: Venitne in mentem tibi quod verbum in cavea dixit histrio: omnes homines ad suom quaestum callent et fastidiunt.
pairs.question: Ad quam rem omnes homines 'callere et fastidire,' secundum verbum histrionis quod Phronesium in Truculento Plauti refert, dicuntur?
pairs.question_en: For what are all men said to be 'shrewd and disdainful,' according to the actor's saying that Phronesium recalls in Plautus' Truculentus?
pairs.derivation: A proverb quoted as a line an actor spoke in the theater (in cavea): all men are cunning for their own gain. Anchored to Truculentus; short answer verbatim (ad suom quaestum callent).

pairs.source_text: Veneris causa adplaudite: eius haec in tutelast fabula.
pairs.question: Cuius deae in tutela fabula Plauti Truculentus, ut epilogus adfirmat, esse dicitur?
pairs.question_en: Under whose divine protection is Plautus' play Truculentus said to be, as the epilogue affirms?
pairs.derivation: A theatrical-convention fact: the epilogue commends the play to Venus' protection ('this play is in her tutelage'), fitting for a comedy of courtesans. Anchored to the named play; one-name answer verbatim (eius haec in tutelast fabula).
